planting.note: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost and transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; like other Brandywine strains, the potato-leaf foliage looks different from typical tomato leaves and the heavy fruit needs sturdy staking.

directions: Transplant into deeply worked, fertile soil in full sun after frost risk passes, and stake or cage the vine early to support the heavy fruit clusters. Black Brandywine belongs to the celebrated Brandywine family of potato-leaf heirloom beefsteaks, distinguished from the classic pink Brandywine by fruit that ripens to a deep purplish-brown to brick-red color with dark green shoulders, carrying the smoky, rich, complex, almost wine-like flavor that 'black' tomatoes are prized for. The large, somewhat irregular fruit can run smaller and less uniform than standard pink Brandywine, a common trait of this style of dark heirloom tomato, but the depth of flavor more than compensates for growers seeking something beyond a standard slicer. Water evenly through fruit development to reduce cracking, and pick as soon as color and give indicate ripeness, since the dark skin can make judging ripeness by color alone trickier than with red tomatoes.

common_name: Brandywine Sudduth's Strain Tomato (Authenticated Original Pink Brandywine)

planting.note: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost and transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; give the sprawling, potato-leaf, long-season vine sturdy staking and plenty of room.

directions: Transplant into rich, well-drained soil in full sun after frost risk passes and provide strong staking, since this vigorous, long-season Brandywine strain produces very heavy fruit over an extended harvest. This is the specific pink Brandywine strain traced to the Sudduth family of Tennessee and distributed to the wider heirloom seed-saving community by collector Ben Quisenberry in the 1980s, and it is widely regarded among heirloom tomato growers as the strain most faithful to the original 19th-century Brandywine. The large, rosy-pink, potato-leaf beefsteak fruit carries the rich, sweet, well-balanced, classically 'old-fashioned' tomato flavor that made Brandywine famous, though yields can run lower and the season longer than modern hybrids. Water consistently and feed moderately through the season, since Brandywine strains are notably more sensitive to inconsistent care than modern disease-resistant hybrids.

common_name: Boxcar Willie Tomato (Reliable Red Beefsteak Heirloom)

planting.note: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost and transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; stake or cage the vigorous indeterminate vine as it grows.

directions: Transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after frost risk passes and stake early to support the productive vine. Boxcar Willie is a widely grown red beefsteak heirloom, said to be named after country singer Boxcar Willie, prized among home gardeners for combining classic large, meaty, smooth, round-oblate red fruit with a more reliable, heavier yield and better disease tolerance than many older large-fruited heirlooms. The mild, well-balanced, classic tomato flavor and consistent fruit set make it a good gateway heirloom for gardeners moving beyond hybrid slicers, and the regular-leaf indeterminate vines keep producing steadily over a long season. Water evenly and feed regularly through fruit set, and stake generously, since the productive vine sets a heavy load of good-sized fruit.

common_name: Livingston's Beauty Tomato (1880s Foundational American Heirloom)

planting.note: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost and transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; stake or cage the indeterminate vine as it grows.

directions: Transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after frost danger passes, staking the vine as it grows. Livingston's Beauty was introduced in 1886 by Alexander W. Livingston of Reynoldsburg, Ohio, one of the most important early tomato breeders in American history, whose systematic selection work through the late 1800s helped transform the tomato from a distrusted curiosity into a smooth, reliably productive garden staple. The medium to medium-large fruit is a rosy pink-red, smooth, and globe-shaped with good, well-balanced flavor for its era — a marked improvement over the ribbed, irregular tomatoes common before Livingston's breeding program, and a variety that directly influenced the smooth, round tomato shape gardeners now take for granted. Grow it as a piece of American horticultural history as much as a garden tomato; water and feed evenly through the season for the best fruit set and flavor.

common_name: Ponderosa Red Tomato (Classic Large Red Potato-Leaf Beefsteak)

planting.note: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost and transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; the heavy, potato-leaf vine needs sturdy staking or caging from an early stage.

directions: Transplant into rich, well-drained soil in full sun after frost risk passes, and stake the heavy vine well before fruit sets. Ponderosa Red is a classic American heirloom beefsteak dating to the late 1800s, grown for very large, deep red, meaty fruit with a dense, low-moisture, few-seeded interior that made it a favorite for slicing thick, generous sandwich rounds long before modern hybrid beefsteaks existed. The potato-leaf foliage typical of Ponderosa strains sets it apart visually from regular-leaf tomatoes, and the plant carries a genuinely old-fashioned, rich tomato flavor prized by heirloom growers over the milder taste of many modern varieties. Water evenly to reduce cracking on the large fruit, and support heavily, since individual tomatoes commonly exceed a pound and can snap unsupported branches.
